rows.reference: Exodus 20:13 (same in Hebrew and English); parallel Deuteronomy 5:17
rows.original: לֹא תִרְצָח (lo tirṣaḥ)
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)
rows.says: Do not murder. The commandment names no victim and sets no limit on who is protected.
rows.bearing: Teaches K1 and K0 (rule 7). The verb rāṣaḥ is used for unlawful killing of a person (and in Numbers 35 also for the unintended manslayer), not for court execution or war, so exclusions (a), (b) and (f) are left to other texts, which fits K1's shape. Translation matters: 'murder' (JPS 1917) is narrower than 'kill' (KJV). Rabbinic law narrows which killings a human court punishes with death (see the limit row on the Mekhilta to Exodus 21:14): graded protection under rule 2, not permission.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: no web search was possible (the shared per-turn search budget was exhausted before this agent's first search); reference and wording from memory, to be checked on Sefaria

rows.reference: Genesis 9:5 to 6 (with 9:3)
rows.original: שֹׁפֵךְ דַּם הָאָדָם בָּאָדָם דָּמוֹ יִשָּׁפֵךְ כִּי בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)
rows.says: Spoken to Noah and his sons: God will require a reckoning for human life from every person, 'even at the hand of every man's brother'. Whoever sheds the blood of a human being shall have his own blood shed, because God made humankind in his image. Verse 3, just before, allows animals to be killed for food.
rows.bearing: Explicit for K1 and K0, as a duty laid on all humankind and protecting every human being (ha-adam) as bearer of the divine image, so it reaches everyone K1 protects (rule 7). 'By man shall his blood be shed' is court punishment in the tradition's reading (Targum Onkelos adds 'with witnesses, by sentence of judges'): context (a). Rabbinic law takes the verse as the source of the universal (Noahide) ban on bloodshed (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 57b), reads 'man within man' to include a fetus for non-Jews (context c), and reads 9:5 as also forbidding suicide (Bava Kamma 91b; context d). Verse 3 (animals) is context (e).

rows.reference: Exodus 21:12 to 14
rows.original: וְכִי יָזִד אִישׁ עַל רֵעֵהוּ לְהָרְגוֹ בְעָרְמָה מֵעִם מִזְבְּחִי תִּקָּחֶנּוּ לָמוּת
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)
rows.says: Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death. If he did not lie in wait and it happened by accident, a place of refuge is provided. But one who wilfully attacks his neighbour to kill him by cunning is taken even from God's altar to die.
rows.bearing: Explicit for K1 and K0: deliberate killing is the gravest wrong, beyond the protection of sanctuary, while accidental killing (exclusion f) is treated apart. The penalty itself is court punishment (context a). Limit: the Mekhilta reads 'his neighbour' (re'ehu) in 21:14 to exclude a non-Jewish victim from the human court's death penalty (graded protection, rule 2; see limit row).

rows.reference: Leviticus 24:17 and 24:21 to 22
rows.original: וְאִישׁ כִּי יַכֶּה כָּל נֶפֶשׁ אָדָם מוֹת יוּמָת ... מִשְׁפַּט אֶחָד יִהְיֶה לָכֶם כַּגֵּר כָּאֶזְרָח
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)
rows.says: Whoever mortally strikes any human being shall be put to death. There is to be one law for the stranger and for the native-born.
rows.bearing: Explicit for K1: 'any human life' (kol nefesh adam), with an equal-law clause in the same passage that covers the resident stranger, so the protection is not limited to Israelites (rule 7). The penalty is court punishment (context a).

rows.reference: Numbers 35:15 to 21 and 35:30 to 34
rows.original: וְלֹא תִקְחוּ כֹפֶר לְנֶפֶשׁ רֹצֵחַ (35:31)
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)
rows.says: Whoever kills with a deadly weapon, or pushes or strikes someone 'of hatred' or 'in enmity' so that he dies, is a murderer. No ransom may be taken for a murderer's life, and shed blood pollutes the land. The refuge law for accidental killing covers the Israelite, the stranger and the settler alike (35:15).
rows.bearing: Explicit for K0: killing out of hatred (be-sin'ah) or enmity (be-eivah) is murder, and no payment can buy it off; also teaches K1. 35:15 places the stranger and settler within the homicide law. The same chapter also lets the avenger of blood kill (see the counter row on Numbers 35:19 to 28).

rows.reference: Deuteronomy 19:4 to 13
rows.original: וְלֹא יִשָּׁפֵךְ דָּם נָקִי ... וּבִעַרְתָּ דַם הַנָּקִי מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)
rows.says: Cities of refuge protect an accidental killer from the avenger of blood, who pursues 'while his heart is hot', since the killer 'was not deserving of death' (19:6), so that innocent blood is not shed (19:10). But if a man hates his neighbour, lies in wait and strikes him dead, the elders fetch him from refuge to die: 'thine eye shall not pity him', and you shall put away the blood of the innocent (19:11 to 13).
rows.bearing: Explicit for K0 (killing out of hatred) and K1. 19:6 shows the Torah itself restraining revenge against an accidental killer, which limits the avenger texts (counter row). The penalty is judicial (context a).

rows.reference: Exodus 23:7
rows.original: וְנָקִי וְצַדִּיק אַל תַּהֲרֹג
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)
rows.says: Keep far from a false charge, and do not kill the innocent and the righteous, for God will not acquit the wicked.
rows.bearing: States 'do not kill the innocent' in so many words, but it stands among rules for witnesses and judges, so its first setting is the court (context a). For private conduct it is Clear teaching of K1 rather than Explicit.

rows.original: אָרוּר לֹקֵחַ שֹׁחַד לְהַכּוֹת נֶפֶשׁ דָּם נָקִי
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)

rows.bearing: Explicit for K0 (killing for gain, as a hired killer) and K1. 'An innocent soul' (nefesh dam naki) carries no limit on the victim; 'his neighbour' in 27:24 raises the usual scope question (rule 7).

rows.original: וְיָדַיִם שֹׁפְכוֹת דָּם נָקִי
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)
rows.says: Among the things God hates are hands that shed innocent blood.
rows.bearing: Explicit for K1: shedding innocent blood is hateful to God, with no limit on the victim; a wisdom saying addressed to everyone.

rows.original: וְגֵר יָתוֹם וְאַלְמָנָה אַל תֹּנוּ אַל תַּחְמֹסוּ וְדָם נָקִי אַל תִּשְׁפְּכוּ בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)
rows.says: To the king of Judah, his servants and his people: do no wrong or violence to the stranger, the orphan and the widow, and do not shed innocent blood in this place.
rows.bearing: Explicit for K1, binding rulers and people alike and naming the most vulnerable, the stranger included (rule 7).

rows.original: קוֹל דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ צֹעֲקִים אֵלַי מִן הָאֲדָמָה
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)
rows.says: God warns the angry Cain that he can master the sin crouching at his door. Cain kills his brother Abel; God says the blood cries out from the ground and curses Cain.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching for K0 (a killing out of anger and envy is condemned) and for K1; told of the first human generation, so not limited to one people.

rows.reference: Genesis 49:5 to 7 (with 34:25 to 31)
rows.original: אָרוּר אַפָּם כִּי עָז וְעֶבְרָתָם כִּי קָשָׁתָה
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)
rows.says: Jacob curses the anger and fury of Simeon and Levi, who 'in their anger slew men' when they killed the men of Shechem to avenge their sister Dinah.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching for K0 (killing in anger and revenge), and the victims were foreigners. Genesis 34 itself ends with the brothers' unanswered question, and Jacob's rebuke there (34:30) is about danger; the moral judgement comes in 49:5 to 7.

rows.original: מִבּוֹא בְדָמִים וְהֹשֵׁעַ יָדִי לִי (25:33)
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)

rows.bearing: Clear teaching for K0: a revenge killing on one's own authority is bloodguilt, and restraint is praised.

rows.original: אֵת אוּרִיָּה הַחִתִּי הִכִּיתָ בַחֶרֶב (12:9)
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)

rows.bearing: Clear teaching for K0: a killing for one's own gain or desire is condemned, even when a king arranges it through others, and the victim is a foreigner. Though carried out by a ruler's order (the form of context a), the text judges it as murder.

rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)

rows.bearing: Clear teaching for K0 (a revenge killing is condemned) and a clear line between killing in war and in peace (context b; bears on K3).

rows.original: וַתְּחַיֶּיןָ אֶת הַיְלָדִים (1:17)
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)

rows.bearing: Clear teaching that newborns are protected from birth (rule 9), and that even a king's order to kill them must be refused.

rows.reference: Leviticus 18:21; 20:2 to 5; Deuteronomy 12:31; 18:10 (with Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:7)
rows.original: כִּי גַם אֶת בְּנֵיהֶם וְאֶת בְּנֹתֵיהֶם יִשְׂרְפוּ בָאֵשׁ לֵאלֹהֵיהֶם (Deuteronomy 12:31)
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled (not checked this run)
rows.says: Do not give any of your children to Molech; whoever does so, Israelite or resident stranger, is put to death, and God sets his face against those who look away. The nations burn their sons and daughters to their gods, an abomination; let no one make a son or daughter pass through fire.
rows.bearing: Explicit ban on parents killing their children by sacrifice (K1, rule 9). Rabbinic law defines the Molech offence by a rite of handing over and passing through fire (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:7), so in that reading Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2 may not be about killing; Deuteronomy 12:31 plainly is.

rows.reference: Psalm 106:37 to 38; Jeremiah 19:4 to 5; Babylonian Talmud Taanit 4a
rows.original: וַיִּשְׁפְּכוּ דָם נָקִי דַּם בְּנֵיהֶם וּבְנוֹתֵיהֶם
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled; Talmud paraphrased from memory
rows.says: They sacrificed their sons and daughters and shed innocent blood, the blood of their own children, and the land was polluted. Jeremiah: they filled this place with the blood of innocents, burning their sons, which God 'commanded not, nor spoke it, neither came it into My mind'. The Talmud applies that last verse to the son of Mesha, to Jephthah's daughter and to Isaac.
rows.bearing: Explicit that killing one's own children is shedding innocent blood (K1, rule 9; parents included). Taanit 4a reads the hard narratives (Genesis 22; Judges 11) as things God never wanted.

rows.original: לֹא תַעֲמֹד עַל דַּם רֵעֶךָ
rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled; Talmud paraphrased from memory
rows.says: Do not stand idly by the blood of your neighbour. The Talmud learns from this the duty to rescue someone drowning or under attack, by force if need be.
rows.bearing: A wider duty to protect life: Clear teaching in K1's direction, and the source (with Deuteronomy 22:26) of the rescuer's part of K1's exception. Scope 're'ekha' (your neighbour) is the usual question (rule 7).

rows.original: נָקֹם יִנָּקֵם
rows.translation: JPS 1917 (content checked against ESV in Article I's research)

rows.translation: Rashi in Hebrew, English as summarised on WideTorah (per Article I); Mekhilta and Talmud not displayed

rows.reference: Leviticus 19:17 to 18 and 19:33 to 34
rows.original: לֹא תִקֹּם וְלֹא תִטֹּר אֶת בְּנֵי עַמֶּךָ
rows.translation: JPS 1917
rows.says: Do not hate your brother in your heart; take no vengeance and bear no grudge against the children of your people, but love your neighbour as yourself. The stranger who lives among you is also to be loved as yourself.
rows.bearing: A wider duty against revenge and hatred that includes K0's 'revenge' and 'hatred' clauses (rule 7). On its own, the no-vengeance clause is owed to 'the children of your people', so it is taught in part; 19:34 extends love as oneself to the resident stranger but does not repeat the vengeance clause.

rows.reference: Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 31a
rows.original: דַּעֲלָךְ סְנֵי לְחַבְרָךְ לָא תַּעֲבֵיד
rows.translation: William Davidson Talmud (Steinsaltz), as recorded in Article I
rows.says: Hillel, to a non-Jew: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow; that is the whole Torah, and the rest is commentary.
rows.bearing: A wider rule that reaches everyone (said to a non-Jew) and includes not killing another for gain, anger, hatred or revenge (K0) and, read as the summary of the law, K1 (rule 7; METHOD section 3, 'Wider rules'). Rabbinic branch only. It is not addressed to killing, so it supports rather than carries the result.

rows.reference: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 37a; Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 4:9 in some numberings)
rows.original: כָּל הַמְאַבֵּד נֶפֶשׁ אַחַת ... מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִלּוּ אִבֵּד עוֹלָם מָלֵא
rows.translation: Own rendering from memory; to be checked against Kulp (Mishnah Yomit) on Sefaria
rows.says: In the warning to witnesses in capital cases: the first human was created alone to teach that whoever destroys a single life is counted as having destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one life a whole world; and for the sake of peace, so that no one can say 'my father is greater than yours'.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching of the worth of each life, grounded in common descent from one person (K1). Its scope turns on a textual variant: printed editions read 'a single life of Israel' (נפש אחת מישראל), while important manuscripts (the Kaufmann manuscript is usually cited) and the Jerusalem Talmud's version are reported to lack 'of Israel'. With the addition it is taught in part (rule 7); without it, it reaches everyone, as the 'my father is greater' clause suggests.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: no web search was possible (shared search budget exhausted); the passage and the manuscript variant are from memory; check on Sefaria and in the Kaufmann manuscript

rows.reference: Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 74a; parallels Pesachim 25b and Yoma 82b
rows.original: מַאי חָזֵית דִּדְמָא דִּידָךְ סוּמָּק טְפֵי
rows.translation: Own rendering from memory; to be checked against the William Davidson Talmud (Steinsaltz)
rows.says: Murder is one of the three acts for which one must let oneself be killed rather than commit it. A man told by a local ruler to kill someone or be killed is told by Rava: be killed and do not kill; who says your blood is redder? Perhaps that man's blood is redder.
rows.bearing: Explicit (Rabbinic) for K1: one may not kill an innocent person even to save one's own life or under a ruler's threat, and the victim is any person ('that man'). The rule binds even someone acting under authority.

rows.reference: Mishnah Niddah 5:3
rows.original: תִּינוֹק בֶּן יוֹם אֶחָד ... וְהַהוֹרְגוֹ חַיָּב
rows.translation: Own rendering from memory; to be checked against Kulp (Mishnah Yomit)
rows.says: A one-day-old infant is a full person in law: among other things it inherits and passes on inheritance, and whoever kills it is liable as a murderer.
rows.bearing: Explicit (Rabbinic) that K1's protection starts at birth (rule 9). Limit: an infant not known to be viable (nefel) is treated differently in court law (Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:2; see limit row).

rows.reference: Mishnah Oholot 7:6
rows.original: יָצָא רֻבּוֹ אֵין נוֹגְעִין בּוֹ שֶׁאֵין דּוֹחִין נֶפֶשׁ מִפְּנֵי נֶפֶשׁ
rows.translation: Own rendering from memory; to be checked against Kulp (Mishnah Yomit)
rows.says: When labour endangers a woman's life, the fetus may be cut up and removed, because her life comes first. Once most of the child (in another reading, its head) has emerged, it may not be touched, because one life is not set aside for another.
rows.bearing: Explicit (Rabbinic) that from birth a child's life weighs the same as anyone's (rule 9). The part before birth is context (c).

rows.reference: Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 56a to 57a; Tosefta Avodah Zarah 8:4 (numbering as recalled)
rows.original: שֶׁבַע מִצְוֹת נִצְטַוּוּ בְּנֵי נֹחַ
rows.translation: Own rendering from memory
rows.says: Seven commandments bind all the descendants of Noah, that is, all humanity; one of them is the ban on bloodshed, learnt from Genesis 9:6.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching that the duty not to murder binds every human being (K1's duty-bearers are everyone). In the same discussion (57a) a Jew who kills a non-Jew is exempt from a human court: graded protection under rule 2 (see limit row).

rows.original: חָבִיב אָדָם שֶׁנִּבְרָא בְצֶלֶם
rows.translation: Own rendering from memory
rows.says: Rabbi Akiva: beloved is every human being, created in the image of God (going on to speak of Israel's special status). Ben Azzai names Genesis 5:1, 'This is the book of the generations of Adam', as a greater principle than 'love your neighbour', because it covers all human beings.

rows.translation: JPS 1917, wording as recalled; Talmud paraphrased from memory
rows.says: The avenger of blood (go'el ha-dam, the victim's kinsman) puts the murderer to death when he meets him. The congregation judges between an accidental killer and the avenger and returns the killer to a city of refuge; if the killer leaves it before the high priest dies and the avenger kills him outside, the avenger bears no bloodguilt. Judicial or private character disputed: Unclear for K1 and K0 (rules 5 and 6). On a strict reading of rule 5 it would be Contradicted in all branches. The refuge law itself, Deuteronomy 19:6 and the king's oath in 2 Samuel 14:11 all restrain the avenger.

support.reconciliation: The Tanakh limits its own hard texts. The cities of refuge restrain the avenger of blood, who pursues 'while his heart is hot' a man 'not deserving of death' (Deuteronomy 19:6 and 19:10; Tier 1). Leviticus 19:18 forbids taking vengeance (Tier 1). The king swears to restrain the avenger (2 Samuel 14:11; Tier 1). Jeremiah 19:5 says God never commanded child sacrifice (Tier 1). In Rabbinic Judaism (Orthodox, and Conservative or Masorti in principle), the Mishnah, the tannaitic midrash and the Talmud are treated as primary. They reconcile by limiting, not by repealing. A burglar at night may be killed only as a presumed threat to life, and a rescuer must use the least force needed (Sanhedrin 72a to 72b and 74a). The avenger of blood is treated as the court's agent (Sanhedrin 45b), and the Talmud disputes how far his permission goes (Makkot 11b to 12a). The zealot's licence is 'the law, but we do not instruct so': it holds only during the act, and it leaves the zealot open to a murder charge or to lawful self-defence by his target (Sanhedrin 81b to 82a). The enticer is tried by a court (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:10). The rebellious son 'never was and never will be' (Sanhedrin 71a). A court that executes often is 'destructive' (Mishnah Makkot 1:10). Killing a slave outright is murder, punished by the sword (Mekhilta; Sanhedrin 52b). Killing a non-Jew is exempt from a human court but left to Heaven (Mekhilta on Exodus 21:14), which is graded protection. The Canaanite and Amalekite commands no longer apply because the nations were mixed up (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4; Berakhot 28a). Taanit 4a reads Jeremiah 19:5 as rejecting the killing of Isaac and of Jephthah's daughter. Below these, the classical commentators and codifiers reconcile but never stand alone (corpus.md: for reconciliation only). Rashi gives the sword penalty for a master who kills his slave. Maimonides covers the non-Jewish victim (Laws of Murder 2:11), codifies the rule about the pit (4:10 to 11), exempts those raised in heresy (Laws of Rebels 3:3), and requires peace first and an open side in sieges (Laws of Kings 5:4 and 6:1 to 7). Later and modern authorities are reported beside the labels and are not counted (decision 7). The Chazon Ish confines the rule about pushing heretics into a pit to an age of evident providence. Menachem Meiri, a medieval authority not on the corpus list, confines laws that distinguish gentiles to the idolaters of antiquity (not verified). Karaite Judaism accepts only the Tanakh, so it has neither the rabbinic limits nor the rabbinic permissions. Its readings of Numbers 25, Numbers 35:26 to 28, Deuteronomy 13, Exodus 21:21 and Exodus 22:1 to 2 were not checked. Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism treat the Talmud and codes as non-binding, and no modern body's statement was checked. None of these reconciliations withdraws Numbers 25:11 to 13, Numbers 35:27, Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 or Avodah Zarah 26b; they narrow them. Every item in this paragraph comes from memory in this run, except Sanhedrin 71a and Rashi on Exodus 21:20, which were verified by search during Article I.

So the label is now Unclear. None of the new support could be verified, so 'Taught' cannot yet be shown (rule 1). On the unverified evidence, the Tier 1 texts teach K1 explicitly and for everyone: Genesis 9:5 to 6, Exodus 20:13, Leviticus 24:17 and 24:22, Exodus 1:17 for newborns and Psalm 106:38 for children. The Rabbinic texts make it explicit from birth, with K1's exact exception: Niddah 5:3, Oholot 7:6, Sanhedrin 8:7, 72a and 74a. Against it, in the Rabbinic branch, Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 (zealots) and Avodah Zarah 26a to 26b (heretics, informers, apostates) let a private person kill someone who threatens no one. The Talmud and later authorities narrow these texts but do not withdraw them (rule 3; decision 7). For all branches, three texts are hard cases. Numbers 25:11 to 13 (Phinehas) and Numbers 35:26 to 28 (the avenger of blood) are disputed as judicial or private, and Exodus 21:21 is disputed as deliberate or not (rules 5 and 6). If these rows verify as recorded, the label is Contradicted in one branch (Rabbinic), and Unclear for the Tanakh that all branches share. If Phinehas or the avenger were read as acting privately under a strict reading of rule 5, the label would be Contradicted in all branches. Karaite readings were not checked.

K0.label: Unclear (provisional); Taught if the avenger of blood is accepted as acting within the court system
K0.reason: Verified so far: Leviticus 19:17 to 18 forbids vengeance and hatred towards 'the children of your people' (taught in part). Leviticus 19:34 extends love to the resident stranger. Shabbat 31a gives everyone a wider rule (Rabbinic). Unverified but strong, and Explicit or Clear teaching for K0: Genesis 9:5 to 6 and Exodus 20:13 (for everyone); Numbers 35:20 to 21 and Deuteronomy 19:11 to 13 (killing in hatred or enmity is murder); Deuteronomy 27:25 (killing for a bribe); 1 Kings 21:19 and 2 Samuel 12:9 (kings who killed for gain); Genesis 4 and 49:5 to 7 (anger); 1 Samuel 25:33 and 1 Kings 2:5 (revenge). The one hard case is Numbers 35:26 to 28. A kinsman who kills an accidental killer outside the city of refuge, 'while his heart is hot' (Deuteronomy 19:6), bears no bloodguilt. The Torah frames this inside a judicial process, and the rabbis treat the avenger as the court's agent. So it is disputed whether the killing is judicial or private (rules 5 and 6), and the label is Unclear. The texts on zealots, heretics and Phinehas concern religious zeal or law, not K0's motives, so they are Implied for K0 and do not decide (rule 4). Exodus 21:21 names no motive. If the avenger of blood is accepted as judicial (context a), K0 is Taught in all branches once the Tier 1 rows are verified.

K3.label: Contradicted (provisional, pending verification)
K3.reason: Deuteronomy 20:16 to 17, 1 Samuel 15:3 and Numbers 31:17 (Tier 1, all branches) command the killing of non-combatants, infants included, in named wars. Yoma 22b (Rabbinic) rejects Saul's appeal to the children's innocence. Rule 2 is applied to K3 as a record wording. The tradition limits these commands but does not withdraw them (decision 7): peace must be offered first, the nations can no longer be identified, and besieged people must be able to flee (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4; Berakhot 28a; Sifrei Numbers 157; Maimonides, Laws of Kings 5:4, 6:1 and 6:7). K3 has support in 2 Kings 6:21 to 23, Amos 1:13, 1 Kings 2:5, and Deuteronomy 20:10 and 20:14. Only Numbers 31:18 is verified (carried over), so formally the texts that decide this are still unverified. They are among the best-known passages of the Tanakh and should verify easily.

rows.reference: Numbers 25:6 to 15 (especially 25:7 to 8 and 25:11 to 13), read with 25:4 to 5
rows.original: בְּקַנְאוֹ אֶת קִנְאָתִי ... בְּרִיתִי שָׁלוֹם
rows.translation: JPS 1917 (wording recalled, not checked in this run)
rows.says: During a plague, while the people weep at the Tent of Meeting, an Israelite chieftain (Zimri, 25:14) brings a Midianite woman (Cozbi, 25:15) into a chamber. Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, follows them and spears both. God says Phinehas turned away divine wrath by being zealous for God, and gives him a 'covenant of peace' and a lasting priesthood. Just before, God told Moses to execute the people's chiefs, and Moses told Israel's judges to kill the men who had joined the worship of Baal of Peor (25:4 to 5).
rows.bearing: K1: two people who were attacking no one are killed by a man holding no court office, and God in the text says the act was right (so rule 4 does not save it). If the killing was private, this is a counted text accepted by every branch that contradicts K1 (rule 2). But its judicial or private character is disputed: 25:5 records a leader's order to judges to kill offenders, Psalm 106:30 can be read as 'executed judgement' (next row), and the Rabbinic reading treats it as zealotry outside any court. Under rule 5 (last sentence) and rule 6 this text alone gives Unclear, not Contradicted. K0: the stated motive is zeal for God, not gain, anger, hatred or revenge, so it does not plainly bear on K0. K3: not an act of war in itself, though 25:16 to 18 then commands war on Midian.

rows.reference: Psalm 106:28 to 31
rows.original: וַיַּעֲמֹד פִּינְחָס וַיְפַלֵּל ... וַתֵּחָשֶׁב לוֹ לִצְדָקָה
rows.translation: JPS 1917 ('wrought judgement'), recalled
rows.says: When the people joined Baal of Peor and a plague broke out, Phinehas stood up and 'wrought judgement' (or 'intervened'), the plague stopped, and this was counted to him as righteousness for all generations.
rows.bearing: K1: confirms at Tier 1, for every branch, God's approval of the act in Numbers 25. The verb vayefallel is disputed: JPS 1917 and KJV render it as judging, which supports a judicial reading; other renderings give 'intervened', and the Talmud (Sanhedrin 44a, reported, unverified) reads it as Phinehas 'contending' with God. rows.translation: Kulp, Mishnah Yomit (recalled, not checked)
rows.says: Three offenders may be struck down by zealots: one who steals a sacred Temple vessel, one who curses by means of sorcery (the wording is obscure), and one who has sexual relations with a non-Jewish (Aramean) woman. In the same mishnah, a priest who serves in the Temple while ritually impure is not brought to court by his fellow priests: the young priests take him outside the courtyard and split his skull with clubs.
rows.bearing: K1: a counted text of the Rabbinic branch lets private persons, outside any court, kill people who are attacking no one, and treats them as not liable. Rule 3: Contradicted in one branch (Rabbinic). The Talmud's narrowing (next rows) keeps the rule as law while refusing to teach it, so it limits but does not remove the permission; on the Article I annex's practice (limits that do not remove a permission leave the label Contradicted) the Rabbinic label stays Contradicted, though an orchestrator could read the narrowing as making it Unclear (rule 6). rows.reference: Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 82a (on Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6)
rows.original: הֲלָכָה וְאֵין מוֹרִין כֵּן
rows.translation: William Davidson Talmud (Steinsaltz), recalled
rows.says: The Gemara narrows the zealots' licence. If a would-be zealot comes to ask, he is not told to act (Rav Hisda): 'it is the law, but we do not instruct so'. The act is allowed only during the offence itself: had Phinehas killed Zimri after he had separated from the woman, Phinehas would have been executed; and had Zimri turned and killed Phinehas, Zimri would not have been executed, because Phinehas counts as a pursuer. The same passage tells that Phinehas reminded Moses of the rule and Moses answered, 'let the one who reads the letter be its agent'.
rows.bearing: The tradition's own counted narrowing of the Phinehas precedent. It limits the licence (no court will authorise it; only during the act; the target may kill the zealot in self-defence) but keeps it as law, so it does not remove the Rabbinic contradiction (rule 3). Moses' reply shows some leader's assent in the story, but the rule is framed as zealotry, not as a court sentence, which supports the private reading of Numbers 25 within the Rabbinic branch.

rows.reference: Numbers 35:19 to 21 and 35:26 to 28, read with 35:12 and 35:22 to 25
rows.original: אֵין לוֹ דָּם
rows.translation: JPS 1917 ('avenger of blood'; 'there shall be no bloodguiltiness for him'), recalled
rows.says: The 'avenger of blood' (go'el ha-dam, the dead person's next of kin) puts a deliberate murderer to death 'when he meeteth him' (35:19, 21). For one who killed without intent, the congregation judges between him and the avenger and returns him to a city of refuge, where he stays until the high priest dies (35:22 to 25). If he goes outside the city's border and the avenger finds and kills him, 'there shall be no bloodguiltiness for him' (35:26 to 27).
rows.bearing: For the deliberate murderer the avenger acts after the congregation's judgement (35:12, 24, 30; Deuteronomy 19:12 has the elders hand him over), so that part is context: court (rule 5). But 35:26 to 27 lets a kinsman, on his own authority and with no court or ruler ordering it, kill a person whom the congregation has found not to be a murderer and who is attacking no one, and declares the killing blameless because of what the victim did (leaving the refuge). This is a counted text accepted by every branch; rule 5 names a kinsman as a private person; so rules 2 and 5 point to Contradicted for K1. It would be Unclear only if the tradition treated the avenger's licence as part of the congregation's sentence (rule 5, last sentence); no such reading was found, though none could be searched in this run. Note that Article I (counter-evidence B) discussed only 35:19 to 21, which is the court case. K0: the text calls the killer 'avenger' (Hebrew go'el, literally redeemer or next of kin) and Deuteronomy 19:6 speaks of his 'hot heart', but it does not make revenge the ground of the licence, and the Rabbinic sages call the killing a duty or a permission; whether it is a killing 'out of revenge' is disputed, so for K0 it is a hard case: Unclear (rule 6). K3: not war.

rows.translation: JPS 1917, recalled
rows.says: Cities of refuge are set up so that the avenger of blood, 'while his heart is hot', does not overtake and kill an unintentional killer who 'was not deserving of death', and so that innocent blood is not shed in the land. A deliberate murderer who flees there is fetched by the elders of his city and handed to the avenger.
rows.bearing: The Torah's own restraint on the avenger: it protects the unintentional killer inside the refuge and makes the deliberate murderer's case a matter for the elders (context: court). It limits but does not remove Numbers 35:26 to 27. For K0 it names the avenger's anger as the danger the law guards against, without forbidding him to kill outside the refuge.

rows.translation: Kulp, Mishnah Yomit (recalled)
rows.says: Roads to the cities of refuge are kept clear, and two Torah scholars go with the unintentional killer in case the avenger tries to kill him on the way, so that they can speak to the avenger (2:5). If the killer goes outside the boundary and the avenger finds him, Rabbi Yose the Galilean says killing him is a duty for the avenger and permitted for anyone else; Rabbi Akiva says it is permitted for the avenger, and anyone else who kills him is liable (2:7).
rows.bearing: The counted Rabbinic reconciliation restrains the avenger (scholars sent to dissuade him) but on both views keeps his licence to kill outside the boundary, and on one view extends it to anyone. So for the Rabbinic branch it confirms Numbers 35:26 to 27 rather than narrowing it away, and does not frame the killing as a court execution (rules 2 and 5).

rows.tier: 1 (verse); Rashi 2 (classical commentator, for reconciliation), following the Mekhilta 2 (treated as primary, Rabbinic)
rows.branch: All branches for the verse; Rabbinic for the reading
rows.reference: Exodus 21:20 to 21; Rashi on Exodus 21:20 and 21:21 (following the Mekhilta and Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 52b)
rows.original: כִּי כַסְפּוֹ הוּא
rows.translation: JPS 1917 (checked in earlier project research against ESV); Rashi as summarised on WideTorah
rows.says: A master who strikes his slave with a rod so that the slave dies 'under his hand' is to be punished ('avenged'), but if the slave survives a day or two the master is not punished, 'for he is his money'. Rashi, following the Mekhilta, reads the punishment as death by the sword (so killing a slave outright is a capital crime) and the exemption as covering a slave who lingers a full day and then dies.
rows.bearing: The slave is protected against being killed outright, on pain of death. The exemption covers a beating followed by delayed death; the text does not say the master meant to kill, and exclusion (f) leaves unintended killing aside. The exemption rests partly on the slave's status ('his money'): graded protection by status (rule 2, last sentence), and for a deliberate killing with delayed death a hard case (rule 6). It does not decide K1 for Judaism on its own; Numbers 35:26 to 27 is the clearer text.

rows.original: אֵין לוֹ דָּמִים
rows.translation: JPS 1917; William Davidson Talmud (Steinsaltz), recalled
rows.says: A thief caught breaking in (by night, as the next verse implies) who is struck and dies brings no bloodguilt on the one who struck him; if the sun has risen on him, there is bloodguilt. The Talmud explains that a burglar is presumed ready to kill an owner who resists, so the householder may act as against an attacker ('if someone comes to kill you, rise early and kill him first'); if it is clear the intruder means no harm to life (its example is a father breaking into his son's house), killing him is forbidden. Rashi reads 'the sun has risen' as 'if it is clear to you that he comes in peace'.
rows.bearing: The tradition reads the verse as defence against a presumed deadly attack, inside K1's exception. On the plain text alone it is a borderline case (killing a burglar at night without proof that he threatened life). Recorded as a limit; not a contradiction on the Rabbinic reading.

rows.reference: Deuteronomy 13:7 to 12 (Hebrew) = 13:6 to 11 (English); Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:10 with Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 67a
rows.original: כִּי הָרֹג תַּהַרְגֶנּוּ יָדְךָ תִּהְיֶה בּוֹ בָרִאשׁוֹנָה
rows.translation: JPS 1917, recalled
rows.says: If even a brother, son, daughter, wife or close friend secretly urges you to worship other gods, do not pity or shield him: 'thou shalt surely kill him; thy hand shall be first upon him to put him to death, and afterwards the hand of all the people', by stoning. Rabbinic law treats the enticer (mesit) as tried by a court on witnesses' evidence (witnesses may even be hidden to catch him), with the witness's hand first as in Deuteronomy 17:7.
rows.bearing: The plain wording could be read as a private or crowd killing of a person who is attacking no one. The Rabbinic reading makes it a court process: context only (rule 5). No reading inside the corpus that makes it a private licence was found, though none could be searched. Outside the corpus: Philo of Alexandria praised immediate private punishment of apostates (Special Laws 1.54 to 57, UNVERIFIED), and the Septuagint reads 'you shall surely report him'. If the judicial or private character is judged disputed, rule 5 gives Unclear.

Rabbinic law gives this only to the Great Sanhedrin of 71 (Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:5), and a baraita says such a city 'never was and never will be' (Sanhedrin 71a; Rabbi Yonatan dissents, saying he saw one). The Rabbinic sources are reported to dispute whether the city's young children are included.

rows.translation: William Davidson Talmud (Steinsaltz), recalled
rows.says: Non-Jews and shepherds of small cattle are neither pulled out of a pit nor pushed into one (no rescue is owed, but they may not be killed). Heretics (minim), informers and apostates are 'lowered and not raised': they may be caused to die.
rows.bearing: K1: a counted Rabbinic text lets private persons cause the death of people who are attacking no one, because of their religious status. Rule 3: Contradicted in one branch (Rabbinic). The informer case overlaps with defence (an informer could endanger lives under a hostile ruler), but heretics and apostates do not. Later authorities limit who counts and suspend the rule (next row), but no counted text withdraws it (METHOD decision 7). For non-Jews the text is graded protection: no killing, no duty of rescue (rule 2). K0: the ground is religious status, not gain, anger, hatred or revenge, so it does not plainly bear.

rows.says: Maimonides codifies the rule that heretics and apostates are 'lowered and not raised', while non-Jews not at war with Israel may not be killed but need not be rescued. He then limits the heretic category: the children and grandchildren of those who deny the oral law (he has the Karaites in view), raised in that belief, are like a child taken captive and are to be drawn back with words of peace, not harmed. The twentieth-century Chazon Ish holds that the rule applied only when divine providence was evident, and that today people are to be drawn back 'with bonds of love'.
rows.bearing: The tradition's own narrowing: classical (Maimonides, reconciliation only) and later (Chazon Ish: counts as reconciliation, never outweighs a counted text). It shrinks and, for today, suspends the Avodah Zarah rule, but the Talmud's text stands. So the Rabbinic label from Avodah Zarah 26b stays Contradicted in one branch, or Unclear if the narrowing is read as leaving the rule's reach unresolved (rule 6).

rows.original: יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוֹי פָּטוּר (printed editions often read עובד כוכבים)

rows.says: Rabbinic law reads 'his neighbour' in Exodus 21:14 as limiting the court's death penalty to the killing of a fellow Israelite. A non-Jew who kills a non-Jew or a Jew is liable, while a Jew who kills a non-Jew is exempt from a human court's death penalty (Sanhedrin 57a). One who meant to kill a non-Jew and killed a Jew is exempt (Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:2).
rows.bearing: Graded protection by faith (rule 2, last sentence): the killing is not made lawful, but the court penalty is withheld. It limits equal protection; it does not contradict K1 so long as the killing stays forbidden, which Maimonides states (next row).

counter.reconciliation:
Judaism has no interpreting body that the project lists as authorised (METHOD decision 8 names only the Universal House of Justice), so its reconciliation comes from three layers, each with a different standing. (1) Counted Rabbinic texts: the Mishnah, Tosefta, tannaitic midrash (Mekhilta, Sifra, Sifrei) and both Talmuds, treated as primary for the Rabbinic branch only (Orthodox, and in principle Conservative or Masorti); Karaites reject them and Reform treats them as non-binding. (2) Classical commentators and codes (Rashi, Tosafot, Maimonides, Ramban, Radak): reconciliation only, never deciding. (3) Later authorities such as the Chazon Ish and Meiri: reconciliation only under METHOD decision 7, never outweighing a counted text. Every item below is UNVERIFIED in this run unless marked.

Zealotry (Phinehas, Numbers 25 and Psalm 106): the counted Rabbinic texts turn the story into a narrow rule (Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6) and then hedge it heavily: a court will not instruct a would-be zealot ('the law, but we do not instruct so'), the act is lawful only during the offence, a zealot who kills afterwards is executed, and the target may kill the zealot as a pursuer (Sanhedrin 82a); the Jerusalem Talmud (Sanhedrin 9:7) says the sages would have excommunicated Phinehas had the holy spirit not intervened. Maimonides (Issurei Biah 12:4 to 5) codifies these limits. The rule is narrowed to the point of near non-use, but it is kept as law, and God's approval in the Tier 1 text stands for every branch.

The avenger of blood (Numbers 35:26 to 27): the Torah restrains the avenger itself (cities of refuge, Deuteronomy 19:6 and 19:10), and the Mishnah sends two scholars with the unintentional killer to dissuade the avenger (Makkot 2:5). But on both views in Mishnah Makkot 2:7 (Rabbi Yose the Galilean: a duty for the avenger; Rabbi Akiva: a permission) the avenger may still kill a manslayer found outside the boundary. No counted or classical text was found that withdraws or judicialises this licence.

Heretics, apostates and informers (Avodah Zarah 26a to 26b): Maimonides keeps the rule but narrows the class (Mamrim 3:3: those raised in heresy, he names the Karaites, are like captured children, to be drawn back with words of peace), and the Chazon Ish (later authority) holds that it does not apply today and that people are to be drawn back with bonds of love. These limit and suspend; no counted text withdraws the rule.

Non-Jews: the Mekhilta, Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:2 and Sanhedrin 57a withhold the court's death penalty from a Jew who kills a non-Jew; Maimonides (Rotzeach 2:11; Avodat Kochavim 10:1) states that such killing is still forbidden while non-Jews are not at war with Israel, and (Kings and Wars 10:12, VERIFIED in earlier research) commands care for non-Jews' sick, dead and poor. This is graded protection, not permission. Tier 1 itself (Genesis 9:6; Leviticus 24:17 and 24:22; Numbers 35:15) does not grade.

Slaves: the Mekhilta and Rashi (VERIFIED in earlier research) make a master who kills his slave outright liable to death, but keep the exemption when the slave lingers a day (Exodus 21:20 to 21): graded protection by status.

Children: the Talmud (Taanit 4a) reads Jeremiah 19:5 as God disowning the offering of Mesha's son, Jephthah's daughter and even Isaac; Genesis Rabbah faults Jephthah's vow; Radak reads Jephthah as not killing his daughter; the Mishnah protects a day-old infant as any person and fixes birth as the point of full protection (Niddah 5:3; Ohalot 7:6). The rebellious son and the city led astray are court matters that the Talmud says never happened (Sanhedrin 71a, VERIFIED in earlier research for the son).

Courts: the enticer of Deuteronomy 13 is tried by a court (Sanhedrin 67a); a court that executes once in seven years is called destructive (Mishnah Makkot 1:10); Rabbinic law also holds that capital jurisdiction ceased with the Sanhedrin about forty years before the Temple's destruction (reported, Avodah Zarah 8b and Sanhedrin 41a).

Defence: the pursuer rule (Mishnah Sanhedrin 8:7; Sanhedrin 73a and 74a) matches K1's exception, demands the least force needed, and forbids killing to prevent idolatry or Sabbath-breaking; 'who says your blood is redder?' (Sanhedrin 74a) forbids killing an innocent person even to save oneself.

War: Maimonides requires peace to be offered first, even to the seven nations and Amalek (Kings and Wars 6:1, VERIFIED in earlier research), a besieged city must be left open on one side (6:7), and the nations are no longer identifiable (5:4; Mishnah Yadayim 4:4); Yoma 22b records Saul's objection on behalf of the children and upholds the command; Tosafot read 'the best of the nations, kill' as about wartime.

Overall the tradition limits rather than repeals. The Tier 1 licence of the avenger of blood and God's approval of Phinehas remain in the text every branch accepts; the Rabbinic counted texts keep the zealot and heretic rules as law while refusing to teach or apply them; Karaite and Reform readings were not checked.

K1.label: Contradicted (provisional: every deciding text is UNVERIFIED in this run, so under rule 1 no label is yet decided)
K1.reason: Numbers 35:26 to 27 (Tier 1, accepted by every branch) lets the dead person's kinsman, on his own authority and with no court or ruler ordering it, kill an unintentional killer found outside his city of refuge, a person who is attacking no one, and declares that 'there shall be no bloodguiltiness for him': rules 2 and 5. Mishnah Makkot 2:7 (Rabbinic) keeps the licence on both views. If the licence were judged part of the congregation's sentence, rule 5 (last sentence) would make this Unclear for all branches; no such reading was found. Phinehas (Numbers 25:7 to 13; Psalm 106:30 to 31, Tier 1, God approves) is Unclear on its own (rules 5 and 6: Numbers 25:5 and the word vayefallel support a judicial reading; the Rabbinic texts call it private zealotry). For the Rabbinic branch there is in addition a Contradicted-in-one-branch result (rule 3) from Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 (zealots; young priests killing an impure priest without a court) and Avodah Zarah 26a to 26b (heretics and apostates 'lowered and not raised'), narrowed but not withdrawn by Sanhedrin 82a, the Jerusalem Talmud, Maimonides and the Chazon Ish. Graded protection only (not contradiction): non-Jews (Sanhedrin 57a; Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:2), slaves (Exodus 21:20 to 21, verified in earlier research) and newborns of doubtful viability (reported). Strong support at Tier 1 (Genesis 9:5 to 6; Exodus 20:13; Exodus 23:7; Leviticus 24:17 and 24:22; Exodus 1; the Molech laws) and in the Mishnah (Niddah 5:3, a day-old infant; Sanhedrin 4:5; 8:7) does not remove a contradiction under rule 2.

K0.label: Unclear (provisional: deciding texts UNVERIFIED in this run)
K0.reason: Tier 1 teaches K0 clearly for every branch: do not murder (Exodus 20:13), cursed is one who takes a bribe to kill an innocent person (Deuteronomy 27:25, the 'for gain' clause), do not take vengeance or bear a grudge (Leviticus 19:18, verified in Article I), do not repay like for like (Proverbs 24:29, verified earlier), and Jacob curses the anger of Simeon and Levi for their revenge killing (Genesis 49:5 to 7). But Numbers 35:26 to 27 licenses the 'avenger of blood' to kill a non-attacker outside the refuge and calls the killing blameless. Whether that is killing 'out of revenge' is disputed: the Hebrew go'el means redeemer or next of kin; the Rabbinic sages call the killing a duty or a permission, not vengeance; Deuteronomy 19:6 names the avenger's 'hot heart' only as the danger that the refuge guards against. That is a disputed word and a hard case (rule 6). If the avenger's killing is counted as revenge, the label becomes Contradicted (all branches). The zealot and heretic rules rest on religious grounds, not gain, anger, hatred or revenge, so they do not plainly bear on K0; Maimonides' justification of the Shechem killing (Kings 9:14, classical, unverified) is reported beside the label and rejected by Ramban.

K3.label: Contradicted (provisional: Deuteronomy 20:16 to 17 and 1 Samuel 15:3 UNVERIFIED in this run; Numbers 31:18 verified in earlier research)
K3.reason: At Tier 1, accepted by every branch, God commands that nothing that breathes be left alive in the cities of the seven nations (Deuteronomy 20:16 to 17) and that Amalek be struck, 'infant and suckling' (1 Samuel 15:3); Moses orders captured Midianite boys and women killed after the battle (Numbers 31:17 to 18). Partial support at Tier 1: in ordinary wars women and children are spared (Deuteronomy 20:14), and Elisha forbids killing captives (2 Kings 6:22). The Rabbinic and classical reconciliation (peace must be offered first, Kings and Wars 6:1, verified earlier; one side of a besieged city left open, 6:7; the nations can no longer be identified, 5:4 and Mishnah Yadayim 4:4) makes the commands inoperative but does not withdraw them, and Yoma 22b upholds the Amalek command against Saul's objection on behalf of the children. K3 is a record wording, not part of the floor.

rows.says: The avenger of blood (go'el ha-dam, the dead person's next of kin) puts a convicted murderer to death (35:19, 21). For one who killed without intent, the congregation judges between him and the avenger and returns him to a city of refuge until the high priest dies (35:22 to 25). If he goes outside its border and the avenger finds and kills him, 'there shall be no bloodguiltiness for him' (35:26 to 27). In 2 Samuel 14 a widow must get the king's oath to stop the avengers killing her son.
rows.bearing: For the convicted murderer the avenger acts after the congregation's judgement, so 35:19 and 35:21 are context (a). But 35:26 to 27 lets a kinsman kill, with no court or ruler ordering it, a person the congregation has found not to be a murderer and who is attacking no one. It declares the killing blameless because of what the victim did (leaving the refuge). This is a counted text accepted by every branch, and rule 5 names a kinsman as a private actor, so rules 2 and 5 give Contradicted for K1 in all branches. The only exception would be a reading within the tradition that makes this killing part of the judicial order (rule 5, last sentence). The support researcher's ground for such a reading, Sanhedrin 45b (the court appoints an avenger where there is none), concerns the convicted murderer of 35:19, not the manslayer outside the refuge. The counted Rabbinic reading of 35:27 itself (Mishnah Makkot 2:7) makes the killing a duty or a permission of the avenger, and on one view of anyone: a private licence. 2 Samuel 14:4 to 11 shows the avenger acting outside any court. No judicial reading was found, but none could be searched, and the Karaite reading was not checked. For K0, whether this is a killing 'out of revenge' is disputed. Go'el means redeemer or next of kin; Deuteronomy 19:6 names his 'hot heart' only as the danger the refuge guards against; Rabbi Yose the Galilean calls the killing a duty. So rule 6 gives Unclear for K0. The refuge law and Deuteronomy 19:6 and 19:10 restrain the avenger but do not withdraw 35:27.

verified.reconciliation: The Tanakh limits its own hard texts. The cities of refuge restrain the avenger of blood, who pursues 'while his heart is hot' a man 'not deserving of death' (Deuteronomy 19:6 and 19:10). David curses Joab's revenge killing (2 Samuel 3:29 and 3:39), and the king can swear to stop avengers (2 Samuel 14:11). Leviticus 19:18 and Proverbs 24:29 forbid revenge, and Jeremiah 19:5 says God never commanded child sacrifice (all Tier 1, all branches). In Rabbinic Judaism (Orthodox, and Conservative or Masorti in principle), the Mishnah, the tannaitic midrash and both Talmuds are counted texts, and they reconcile by limiting rather than repealing. A burglar may be killed only as a presumed threat to life, and a rescuer must use the least force needed (Sanhedrin 72a to 72b and 74a). The zealot's licence is 'the law, but we do not instruct so': it holds only during the act, a zealot who kills afterwards is executed, and his target may kill him as a pursuer (Sanhedrin 81b to 82a). The Jerusalem Talmud says the sages would have excommunicated Phinehas (Sanhedrin 9:7). Scholars escort the manslayer to dissuade the avenger (Mishnah Makkot 2:5), but both views in Mishnah Makkot 2:7 keep the avenger's licence outside the refuge. The enticer is tried by a court (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:10). The rebellious son and the city led astray 'never were and never will be' (Sanhedrin 71a, verified for the son). A court that executes often is 'destructive' (Mishnah Makkot 1:10), and capital jurisdiction is held to have ended in antiquity. Killing a slave outright is a capital crime (Mekhilta and Sanhedrin 52b, seen only through Rashi). Killing a non-Jew is exempt from a human court but left to Heaven (Mekhilta on Exodus 21:14), which is graded protection. The Canaanite and Amalekite commands can no longer be applied because the nations were mixed up (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4). Taanit 4a reads Jeremiah 19:5 as rejecting the killing of Isaac and of Jephthah's daughter. Below these, the classical codifiers reconcile but never decide (corpus.md). Maimonides forbids killing non-Jews not at war with Israel and commands care for their sick, dead and poor (Kings and Wars 10:12, verified). He exempts those raised in heresy from the pit rule (Mamrim 3:3), codifies the zealot limits (Issurei Biah 12:4 to 5), and requires peace to be offered first even to the seven nations (Kings and Wars 6:1, verified), with one side of a besieged city left open (6:7). Later authorities are reported but do not count against a counted text (decision 7). The Chazon Ish holds that the pit rule does not apply today. Karaite Judaism accepts only the Tanakh, so it has neither the rabbinic limits nor the rabbinic permissions, and its readings of Numbers 25, Numbers 35:26 to 28, Deuteronomy 13, Exodus 21:21 and Exodus 22:1 to 2 were not checked. Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism treat the Talmud and codes as non-binding; no statement of any modern body was checked. None of these reconciliations withdraws Numbers 35:27, Numbers 25:11 to 13, Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6, Avodah Zarah 26b or Deuteronomy 20:16; they narrow them. Everything in this paragraph is UNVERIFIED in this run, except where marked verified (carried over from earlier project research).

K1.label: Unclear on verified rows (rule 1); provisionally Contradicted in all branches if Numbers 35:26 to 27 verifies as recorded
K1.reason: Rule 1 lets only verified counted texts decide. The verified rows are Exodus 21:20 (slaves killed outright are protected), Exodus 21:21 (a hard case: a death after a beating left unpunished 'for he is his money', with no stated intent to kill; rule 6) and Shabbat 31a (Rabbinic only; its reach is narrowed by Rashi's second reading). On these the label is Unclear. No verified text accepted by all branches teaches K1 for everyone, and none plainly contradicts it. On the unverified rows, Tier 1 teaches K1 explicitly and for everyone (Genesis 9:5 to 6; Exodus 20:13; Leviticus 24:17 and 24:22; Exodus 1:17 for newborns; Psalm 106:38 for children), and the Mishnah protects a day-old infant (Niddah 5:3). Against this, Numbers 35:26 to 27, accepted by every branch, lets the dead person's kinsman, with no court or ruler ordering it, kill a manslayer found outside his city of refuge, a person attacking no one, and declares 'no bloodguilt'. Rule 5 names a kinsman as a private actor, and rule 2 covers a killing declared blameless because of what the victim did. So once verified this gives Contradicted in all branches. It would drop to Unclear only if a reading within the tradition makes the killing part of the court's sentence (rule 5, last sentence). The support researcher's ground for that (Sanhedrin 45b) concerns the convicted murderer of 35:19, and the counted Rabbinic reading of 35:27 (Mishnah Makkot 2:7) is a private licence. The Karaite reading was not checked. Phinehas (Numbers 25:7 to 13; Psalm 106:30 to 31) is Unclear for all branches, because whether it was judicial or private is disputed (rules 5 and 6). Whatever happens to Numbers 35, the Rabbinic branch is in any case Contradicted in one branch (rule 3), from Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 (zealots; young priests killing an impure priest without a court), Avodah Zarah 26a to 26b (heretics and apostates 'lowered and not raised') and Mishnah Makkot 2:7. The Talmud, Maimonides and the Chazon Ish narrow these but do not withdraw them (decision 7). Graded protection only, not contradiction: non-Jews (Sanhedrin 57a; Mekhilta), slaves dying after a day (Rabbinic reading of Exodus 21:21), newborns of doubtful viability, and the treifah. Of the deciding texts, only Exodus 21:20 to 21 is verified.

Shabbat 31a (Rabbinic) is a wider rule covering all four motives, but its reach is narrowed by a classical commentator (rule 6). No verified text covers gain, anger and hatred for everyone in all branches, so on verified rows K0 is taught in part only. No verified counter-evidence bears on K0, since Exodus 21:21 names no motive. On the unverified rows, Tier 1 teaches every clause for every branch: hatred (Numbers 35:20 to 21; Deuteronomy 19:11 to 13), gain (Deuteronomy 27:25; 1 Kings 21:19; 2 Samuel 12:9), anger (Genesis 4; Genesis 49:5 to 7) and revenge (1 Samuel 25:33; 2 Samuel 3:39; 1 Kings 2:5 and 2:31). The one hard case is Numbers 35:26 to 27. Whether the kinsman's licensed killing of the manslayer outside the refuge is a killing 'out of revenge' is disputed: go'el means redeemer or next of kin; Deuteronomy 19:6 names his 'hot heart' only as the danger the refuge guards against; and Rabbi Yose the Galilean calls it a duty. That gives Unclear (rule 6). If the killing is counted as revenge, K0 is Contradicted in all branches; if not, Taught in all branches. The zealot, heretic, informer and Phinehas texts rest on religious or communal grounds, not K0's motives, so they do not decide K0. Whether Karaite law keeps or restricts the avenger's licence is the single most important unchecked branch question. The Tanakh still applies to them under the method's text test, but none of their own statements or platforms was checked. verified.fairness_notes: 1. Size and candour of the corpus. Judaism's counted Rabbinic corpus is very large, and it openly records minority views, hard cases and its own narrowings. A tradition with a short canon has fewer chances to be found 'Contradicted in one branch'. The rules are the same, but adherents may feel that dormant law is being judged as if it were live permission. Examples: the zealot rule is 'the law, but we do not instruct so'; the pit rule is suspended (Chazon Ish); capital jurisdiction ended in antiquity; the rebellious son and the city led astray 'never were'. The article should say plainly that decision 7 is applied the same way to every tradition with dormant or suspended rules (for example the apostasy and hudud hadith in Islam, the Manusmriti, and the Christian Old Testament's judicial law). It should also always report these narrowings beside the label. 2. Shared Tier 1 with Christianity. Numbers 35:26 to 27, Numbers 25, Exodus 21:21, Deuteronomy 20:16 and 1 Samuel 15:3 are also in the Christian Old Testament. If Judaism is labelled Contradicted in all branches on Numbers 35:27, Christianity must be labelled the same way unless one of its counted texts withdraws the law. A Christian Tier 2 reconciliation (for example Aquinas on the end of the judicial precepts) must get no more weight than Rabbinic or Maimonidean reconciliation gets here. 3. Like cases elsewhere. The avenger of blood should be compared openly with retaliation by heirs in other traditions (for example Islamic qisas carried out under a ruler's authority). Only the killing of the manslayer outside the refuge, with no court order, is treated as private here, and the same test should be shown for every tradition. Graded protection for non-Jews (Sanhedrin 57a) must be labelled the same as comparable rules elsewhere (for example the hadith that a Muslim is not killed for a non-Muslim, and caste-graded penalties in the Hindu law books): graded protection, not contradiction. 4. Translation. Rendering go'el ha-dam as 'avenger of blood' builds in the 'revenge' reading that decides K0, and 'murder' against 'kill' for lo tirṣaḥ narrows or widens Exodus 20:13. Recommend adding go'el ha-dam to the 'Where translation changes meaning' list in sources/translations.md. 5. Presentation. Avodah Zarah 26b and Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 should never be quoted without the limits the tradition itself sets and the fact that no living branch applies them. Phinehas should be shown with the Jerusalem Talmud's disapproval. 6. Narratives (Genesis 22, Judges 11, Genesis 38, 2 Kings 2, 1 Kings 18:40) are treated as Implied under rule 4, the same standard as narratives in other traditions; the Tanakh's own condemnation of revenge killings (Genesis 49:5 to 7; 2 Samuel 3:39; 1 Kings 2:31) should be given equal space.
